title: Compute the Nth Fibonacci number, where each number is the sum of the two preceding ones. Explain the Fibonacci Numbers dynamic programming pattern, bottom-up versus memoization, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Fibonacci Numbers (Compute the Nth Fibonacci with Dynamic Programming)

s1_definition.profdef: Fibonacci Numbers is the foundational problem of the Fibonacci Numbers dynamic programming pattern, where each state depends on a fixed number of previous states. We compute it bottom-up by keeping only the last two values, giving linear time and constant space, or top-down with memoization to avoid the exponential recomputation of naive recursion.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India models a simple compounding sequence where each month's figure is the sum of the previous two months. The Fibonacci pattern computes the Nth figure efficiently by remembering just the last two months instead of recomputing the whole history each time.
s1_definition.oneliner: Each state depends on the previous two; keep two running values for linear time and constant space.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Fibonacci Numbers is the foundational problem of the Fibonacci Numbers dynamic programming pattern, where each state depends on a fixed number of previous states. We compute it bottom-up by keeping only the last two values, giving linear time and constant space, or top-down with memoization to avoid the exponential recomputation of naive recursion.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India models a simple compounding sequence where each month's figure is the sum of the previous two months. The Fibonacci pattern computes the Nth figure efficiently by remembering just the last two months instead of recomputing the whole history each time.

**One line to remember:** Each state depends on the previous two; keep two running values for linear time and constant space.

sections.s2_technical:
The definition is that the zeroth Fibonacci is zero, the first is one, and every later one is the sum of the two before it. Naive recursion recomputes the same subproblems exponentially, so we apply dynamic programming.

The bottom-up method keeps two variables, the previous two Fibonacci values, and iterates forward: `int prev2 = 0, prev1 = 1; for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) { int cur = prev1 + prev2; prev2 = prev1; prev1 = cur; }`. The result is `prev1` for n at least one. This is linear time and constant space because we never store the whole array. The memoization method caches each computed value in a map or array and returns the cached value on repeat calls, turning the exponential recursion into linear work. Senior nuance: for very large n the values overflow long quickly, so a real system would use BigInteger, and the pattern generalizes to any recurrence with a fixed-size window of previous states, which is why it is treated as its own DP family.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a modelling tool where a projected figure for each period is the sum of the previous two periods, a simple recurrence the analytics team uses for illustration. Computing the Nth figure with naive recursion is far too slow for large N because it recomputes the same periods repeatedly. This is exactly how the Fibonacci Numbers pattern works: it computes the Nth term in linear time by remembering recent terms.

The code defines a `SequenceModelService` exposing `fib(n)` using the bottom-up two-variable method and returning the Nth figure. A `Demo` computes a sample term and logs it.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is n equal to ten. We want the tenth figure in the sequence zero, one, one, two, three, five, and so on.

Step 1 — Since n is at least two, we start with prev2 equal to zero and prev1 equal to one, representing the zeroth and first terms.

Step 2 — For i equal to two, the current term is one plus zero equals one. We shift: prev2 becomes one, prev1 becomes one. The second term is one.

Step 3 — For i equal to three, current is one plus one equals two. Shift: prev2 one, prev1 two. For i equal to four, current is two plus one equals three. Shift: prev2 two, prev1 three.

Step 4 — Continuing, the terms become five, eight, thirteen, twenty-one, thirty-four as i climbs through five, six, seven, eight, nine, each time summing the last two and shifting.

Step 5 — For i equal to ten, current is thirty-four plus twenty-one equals fifty-five. The tenth figure is fifty-five, held in prev1. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:27:50 PM com.bank.sequence.service.SequenceModelService fib
INFO: fib(10) = 55
Oct 27, 2026 9:27:50 PM com.bank.sequence.SequenceModelApplication main
INFO: The 10th sequence figure is 55
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Fibonacci Numbers is the foundational problem of the Fibonacci Numbers dynamic programming pattern, a family where each state depends on a small fixed window of previous states. The zeroth term is zero, the first is one, and each later term is the sum of the two before it. Naive recursion recomputes the same subproblems an exponential number of times, so I apply dynamic programming.

I prefer the bottom-up method because it needs only constant space. I keep two variables for the previous two terms and iterate forward, computing each new term as their sum and then sliding the window by shifting the variables. That gives linear time and constant space. The alternative is top-down memoization, where I cache each computed term so repeated recursive calls return instantly, which also collapses the exponential work to linear. For large indices the values outgrow a long quickly, so a production system would switch to BigInteger.

At the National Bank of India I used this pattern in a modelling tool where a projected figure for each period was the sum of the previous two periods, and the analytics team needed the Nth figure fast for large N. I used the two-variable bottom-up computation rather than naive recursion. Explaining that each state depends only on the last two, that bottom-up gives constant space while memoization gives linear time from caching, and that large indices need BigInteger is what shows an interviewer I understand the Fibonacci Numbers DP pattern and its practical limits.
